woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The anti-fascist themes are the continuation of a storyline established across two full seasons of television. Tim Roth's fascist villain Beckett is a direct successor to Sam Claflin's Oswald Mosley. There is nothing smuggled in. The marketing, the trailers, and every interview with Steven Knight and Cillian Murphy have been transparent about the WWII setting and the fascist antagonist. Conservative viewers who enjoyed Seasons 5 and 6 will find familiar territory. Murphy himself has explicitly rejected preachy filmmaking.

director.name: Tom Harper
director.ideology: NEUTRAL. Harper grew up in a Quaker family and credits Quakerism with shaping his attitudes toward equality and fairness, but his filmography shows no consistent ideological pattern. Wild Rose (2018) is a working-class uplift story about a single mother pursuing her country music dream. The Aeronauts (2019) is a period adventure. War and Peace (2016) is a faithful Tolstoy adaptation. He directed the back half of Peaky Blinders Season 1, establishing the show's visual language alongside cinematographer George Steel. His return to the franchise is a creative homecoming, not an ideological appointment.
director.profile: British film and television director born January 7, 1980. Grew up in a Quaker household. Studied at the National Film and Television School. His early career included BBC television work before breaking through with Wild Rose, which earned Jessie Buckley a BAFTA nomination. The Aeronauts starred Eddie Redmayne and Felicity Jones. Harper directed episodes of Peaky Blinders Season 1 and returns to close the saga alongside cinematographer George Steel, who also shot Season 1. Murphy specifically requested Harper for the film, citing trust and their shared understanding of the Peaky Blinders visual world.

writer.name: Steven Knight
writer.profile: Birmingham-born writer, producer, and creator of Peaky Blinders. Knight is one of British television's most prolific and commercially successful writers. He co-created Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, wrote the screenplays for Dirty Pretty Things (2002), Eastern Promises (2007), Locke (2013), Spencer (2021), and See (Apple TV+). He created the series Taboo with Tom Hardy. Knight drew on his own family history for Peaky Blinders - his father worked in Digbeth, Birmingham, shoeing police horses, and his mother lived through the Birmingham Blitz that forms the backdrop of this film. He built Digbeth Loc. Studios in Birmingham specifically to house this production. Knight has written all 36 hours of Peaky Blinders television and the film screenplay solo. His storytelling sensibility is working-class, masculine, and rooted in the specific texture of Birmingham's industrial history.

lead_producer.name: Steven Knight, Cillian Murphy, Caryn Mandabach, Guy Heeley, Jimmy Tandel
lead_producer.company: Garrison Drama / Nebulastar / BBC Film / Netflix

composer.name: Martin Phipps / Various
composer.profile: The Peaky Blinders franchise is known for its anachronistic use of modern music over period imagery - Nick Cave's 'Red Right Hand' serves as the series' theme song and returns in a subtle callback in the film. Music supervision has always been central to the show's identity, layering Arctic Monkeys, PJ Harvey, and Radiohead over 1920s-1940s Birmingham. The film continues this tradition.

fidelityCasting.assessment: This is a direct continuation of the Peaky Blinders television series, and the casting reflects strict fidelity to the established characters. Cillian Murphy returns as Tommy Shelby. Sophie Rundle returns as Ada. Ned Dennehy returns as Charlie Strong. Packy Lee returns as Johnny Dogs. Ian Peck returns as Curly. Stephen Graham returns as Hayden Stagg. The only notable recast is Barry Keoghan replacing Conrad Khan as the adult Duke Shelby, Tommy's illegitimate son introduced in Season 6. This is an age-appropriate recast - Keoghan plays the character years later as a grown man. The new characters (Rebecca Ferguson's Kaulo, Tim Roth's Beckett, Jay Lycurgo's Elijah Hayes) are original additions to the story, not replacements for existing characters. No race-swapping. No gender-swapping. No ideological recasting. The Peaky Blinders universe remains intact.

parentalGuidance.guidance: Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man is a continuation of a TV-MA television series and carries the same content expectations. Violence is intense but purposeful, advancing the narrative rather than existing for shock value. The father-son conflict between Tommy and Duke provides genuine dramatic tension that could be disturbing for viewers with family trauma. The fascist villain's plan involves Nazi counterfeit operations using concentration camp labor - this is historically inspired by Operation Bernhard and is referenced rather than graphically depicted. Tommy's opium use is presented as self-destructive, not glamorized. This is a film for adults and mature older teenagers who are familiar with the series. Not appropriate for younger teens.

summary.overall:
Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man delivers exactly what its six seasons of television promised: a masculine, violent, morally complex crime drama about a deeply flawed man who comes out of hiding to save his son, fight fascists, and protect his family during Britain's darkest hour. The film works both as a conclusion for longtime fans and as a standalone piece for newcomers, and it does so without a single moment of progressive preachiness.

The year is 1940. The Luftwaffe is bombing Birmingham. A BSA factory in Small Heath explodes, killing Agnes Shelby, a previously unseen family member. Tommy Shelby (Cillian Murphy) is living in rural exile, smoking opium and writing his memoir on a typewriter, haunted by the ghost of his dead daughter Ruby. He has abandoned everything - his empire, his family, his name. When his sister Ada (Sophie Rundle), now an MP, arrives to tell him that his illegitimate son Duke (Barry Keoghan) has reformed the Peaky Blinders and is 'running them like it is 1919 all over again,' Tommy refuses to engage.

Duke is the film's most compelling creation. Keoghan plays him with feral, unpredictable energy - a young man who inherited his father's ambition but not his discipline, raised without a father and now filling that void with violence and power. Tim Roth's Beckett, Treasurer of the British Union of Fascists, sees in Duke the perfect recruit. Beckett's plan is staggering in scope: smuggle 350 million pounds in Nazi counterfeit notes into Britain to collapse the economy, with Duke taking a 20% cut in exchange for assassinating his aunt Ada. The historical inspiration - Operation Bernhard, which actually produced counterfeit British notes using concentration camp labor - grounds the plot in reality.

Tommy is finally drawn back into the world by Rebecca Ferguson's Kaulo, a Romani woman with psychic abilities and the twin sister of Duke's dead mother. Kaulo connects Tommy to his Romani heritage and destiny in ways that Ada's political appeals could not. Ferguson plays the role with mysterious intensity, and her character serves the same function as the supernatural feminine figures who have appeared throughout the series - Polly Gray's visions, the fortune-tellers, the ghosts. This is not girl-boss feminism; it is the ancient archetype of the wise woman who sees what men cannot.

The reunion between father and son is the film's centerpiece. Deadline's review describes 'an impressive brawl in pig sh*t that ruins Tommy's fine tailoring' as the precursor to an uneasy truce. The Oedipal tension between Duke and Tommy drives the narrative toward a climax that hinges on whether Duke will betray his country or his father. Steven Knight structures this as a race against time - 'Everything is happening at midnight!' - but the real clock is ticking on a father's last chance to save his son.

The traditional values are embedded in every frame. Fatherhood as duty and obligation - Tommy abandoned Duke and the film treats this as a catastrophic failure with real consequences. Patriotism against genuine fascism - not contemporary political allegory but actual WWII-era treason and collaboration. Masculine competence restored through action - Tommy returns to form in what Deadline calls 'an exquisite moment' when the old Tommy resurfaces at the Garrison Tavern. Family loyalty as the organizing principle of morality - the Shelby clan reassembles around Tommy not because of ideology but because blood demands it.

Murphy brings an unexpectedly emotional flourish to a character he has played for 13 years. The memoir framing device is occasionally heavy-handed - Deadline notes that 'the sight of Tommy continuing to tap away at the keyboard while riding on a canal barge is borderline laughable' - but once he gets into gear, Murphy's Tommy is as magnetically dangerous as ever. He reportedly bulked up from his gaunt Oppenheimer frame, making Tommy feel physically imposing again.

The woke content is minimal and entirely organic to the source material. The anti-fascist theme is historically patriotic, not politically allegorical. Fighting actual Nazis in 1940 is what Churchill, Eisenhower, and every Allied soldier did. Ada's role as an MP reflects her six-season character arc. Ferguson's supernatural feminine character follows established Peaky Blinders tradition. Some progressive commentators have tried to claim the show as anti-capitalist, anti-masculine critique, but as Deadline notes, the film 'knows exactly what it is' - British pulp entertainment in the tradition of spaghetti Westerns and wartime adventure comics.

Cillian Murphy stated in a Telegraph interview: 'The last thing I want to be involved in is preachy or dogmatic work because films should never tell you how to feel.' In 2026 Hollywood, that philosophy is itself a traditional value.

Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man is a rare beast: a prestige production that respects masculine archetypes, celebrates family loyalty, treats patriotism as an unquestioned good, and refuses to moralize. It is one of the most satisfying films of early 2026 for conservative audiences, and it earns its STRONGLY TRADITIONAL verdict without qualification.
wokeElements: The anti-fascist theme, while historically grounded in actual WWII, invites contemporary interpretation - Tim Roth noted 'fascism comes at you in many disguises, as we know,' the 'as we know' implying modern parallels

Rebecca Ferguson's Kaulo has supernatural psychic powers and drives Tommy out of exile - adjacent to the 'mystical woman who knows more than the men' trope, though established within the show's existing supernatural tradition

Ada Shelby as a female Member of Parliament in 1940 Britain, while historically possible, places her in a position of political authority that the film uses to deliver some progressive perspectives through a period-appropriate vessel
The film's Romani cultural reverence, while organic to the series since Season 1, aligns with contemporary representation priorities
The counterfeit operation uses concentration camp labor - while historically accurate, this thematic element engages with Holocaust memory in ways that carry contemporary political weight
tradElements: Father-son redemption as the central dramatic engine - Tommy abandoned Duke, Duke became violent and vulnerable to fascist manipulation, Tommy must return to save his son and face the consequences of his abandonment
Wartime patriotism treated as an unquestioned good - fighting WWII-era fascism is presented as duty, not moral complexity, with treason against Britain depicted as genuine evil
Family loyalty as the highest moral value - the Shelby clan reassembles around Tommy because blood demands it, not because of ideology or politics
Masculine competence celebrated without deconstruction - Tommy's intelligence, physical toughness, and strategic cunning are the tools that save his son and country
Consequences of abandonment presented without excuse - Tommy's failure as a father created the crisis he must now resolve, reinforcing that fathers who walk away create broken men
Working-class identity and regional pride as central values - Steven Knight built a studio in Birmingham to tell Birmingham stories with Birmingham textures
The villain is a fascist collaborator committing treason - evil is clearly delineated and physically confronted rather than merely debated
Cillian Murphy's explicit rejection of preachy filmmaking - 'films should never tell you how to feel' - reflects an entertainment-first philosophy increasingly rare in prestige cinema
summary.adultInsight:
Conservative adults should approach The Immortal Man with high confidence. This is one of the most culturally satisfying prestige productions of 2026 for traditional audiences. The WWII anti-fascist framing is historically patriotic, not politically allegorical. Murphy's public rejection of preachy filmmaking is a reliable signal. The creative team is the same writer (Knight) and director (Harper from Season 1) who built the franchise. The cast is stacked with proven talent. The production shot practically with real explosions rather than relying on CGI. Tim Roth praised it: 'It properly feels like an old Second World War movie. It had ambition.'

For viewers unfamiliar with the TV series: the film works as a standalone story. Deadline confirms that 'strangers won't be too overwhelmed by backstory.' The essential dynamics - father vs. son, loyalty vs. treason, family vs. fascism - are universal enough to land without six seasons of context.

Netflix streaming release on March 20 if you prefer to skip the limited theatrical run on March 6.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R for strong violence, pervasive language, and drug use. Recommended age: 16 and up. This is a continuation of a TV-MA series known for intense gang violence, strong language, and mature content. The film features WWII bombing sequences with civilian casualties, gang violence, a brutal fight in a pig pen, and the moral complexity the series is known for. Tommy's opium use is part of his self-destructive arc, not glamorized. Not appropriate for children or young teenagers. Mature teens who have watched the series will find familiar territory. Discussion-worthy topics include the consequences of absent fathers, how fascism recruits young men through appeals to power, and whether bad men can do good things.

representation.notes: The cast is predominantly white British and Irish, consistent with the show's 1940 Birmingham setting. Jay Lycurgo (British-Trinidadian) as Elijah Hayes is the most prominent non-white addition, but his casting raises no fidelity concerns as an original character. The Romani representation is organic to the source material. No demographic engineering.

messaging.notes: The anti-fascist message is historically grounded rather than allegorical. The film does not draw explicit contemporary parallels. Tim Roth's comment about fascism's disguises ('as we know') is the closest thing to a modern political reference, and it comes from a press interview rather than the film itself.

gender_portrayal.notes: Ada Shelby as an MP and Rebecca Ferguson's psychic Kaulo are the primary female characters. Both are powerful but neither is framed as a girlboss. Ada's authority is earned across six seasons. Kaulo follows the show's established tradition of supernatural feminine figures. Tommy, Duke, Beckett, and the male Shelby clan dominate the narrative.

family_values.notes: Family loyalty is the spine of the entire film. Tommy returns for his son. The Shelby clan reassembles. The consequences of Tommy's abandonment are presented as catastrophic. The resolution requires a father to step up and a son to choose family over power. This is as pro-family as prestige cinema gets.

faith_portrayal.notes: Faith is not a primary theme, but the Romani spiritual elements (Kaulo's psychic abilities, Tommy's ghosts) are presented with reverence rather than mockery. The show has always treated supernatural elements as real within its universe.

tropeAudit.name: Father-Son Redemption
tropeAudit.description: The entire dramatic engine of The Immortal Man is Tommy Shelby returning from exile to save his estranged son Duke from self-destruction and fascist manipulation. Tommy abandoned Duke. Duke grew up without a father and is now running the Peaky Blinders with reckless violence, tempted by a fascist to commit treason. Tommy must reclaim his parental authority and pull his son back from the edge. Steven Knight explicitly described the father-son dynamic as the film's main structure. The Oedipal overtones are acknowledged by Deadline's review.

tropeAudit.name: Wartime Patriotism and Duty
tropeAudit.description: Tommy Shelby returns not just for his son but for his country. The film is set during the Blitz, when Britain faced existential threat from Nazi Germany. The central political conflict is whether Duke will commit treason by siding with the fascists or stand with Britain. Tommy, a WWI veteran who has seen the cost of war firsthand, chooses to fight again. The film treats wartime service and national loyalty as unambiguous goods.

tropeAudit.name: Family Loyalty as Highest Value
tropeAudit.description: The Shelby clan reassembles around Tommy - Charlie Strong, Johnny Dogs, Curly - because blood demands it. Ada rallies Tommy by telling him what Duke is doing. The family unit is the organizing principle of the narrative, and loyalty to it overrides personal safety and self-interest.

tropeAudit.name: Masculine Competence Under Pressure
tropeAudit.description: Tommy Shelby is the archetype of masculine competence. The film features large-scale practical action with real explosions and period vehicles. Murphy bulked up physically for the role. The production ethos is classic WWII cinema - Roth compared it to 'Gregory Peck and Richard Burton up a mountain somewhere.' Deadline describes the film as having 'shades of Sergio Leone's spaghetti Westerns' in its final showdown.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences of Abandonment
tropeAudit.description: Tommy abandoned his son. The direct consequence is that Duke grew up wild, violent, and vulnerable to fascist recruitment. The film does not excuse Tommy's abandonment or frame it as self-care. It presents it as a failure with real consequences that Tommy must now face. Fathers who abandon their children create broken men, and the only remedy is to return and do the hard work of fatherhood.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Fascism with Modern Resonance
tropeAudit.description: The anti-fascist theme is historically accurate - the British Union of Fascists was a real organization, and wartime fascist sympathizers were a real domestic threat. Tim Roth's comment that 'fascism comes at you in many disguises, as we know' invites a modern parallel but the film itself stays anchored in 1940. This is historically patriotic anti-fascism, not contemporary political commentary.

tropeAudit.name: Supernatural Feminine Power
tropeAudit.description: Rebecca Ferguson's Kaulo is a Romani woman with psychic abilities who drives Tommy out of retirement. She represents the show's longstanding tradition of supernatural feminine figures (Polly Gray's visions, the fortune-tellers). Knight wanted her to 'reflect the tradition of powerful female characters and the fact that Peaky has always been a bit supernatural.' This predates modern feminism by centuries in storytelling tradition.

tropeAudit.name: Female Political Authority
tropeAudit.description: Ada Shelby has become an MP. This reflects her character arc across six seasons - she was always the most politically engaged Shelby. The progression from activist to elected official is narratively earned. A female MP in 1940 Britain is historically possible (women MPs existed from 1919), and Ada's authority is never used to undermine the male characters.

comparison_films.title: The Godfather Part III (1990)
comparison_films.comparison: The most relevant structural comparison. Both films are about aging crime bosses who come out of retirement to save their families. Both feature the father-son/father-daughter dynamic as the emotional core. Both deal with betrayal from within the family's circle. The Immortal Man is a stronger film than Part III because Tommy's son is a more compelling antagonist than Vincent Corleone, and Murphy's return to the role is more convincing than Pacino's.

comparison_films.title: Dunkirk (2017)
comparison_films.comparison: Christopher Nolan's WWII film shares The Immortal Man's reverence for wartime sacrifice and practical filmmaking. Both films treat the war as backdrop for human stories about duty and survival. Both directors insisted on practical effects over CGI. Nolan's film is more technically ambitious; Harper's is more emotionally intimate.

comparison_films.title: Road to Perdition (2002)
comparison_films.comparison: Sam Mendes' film about a hitman trying to save his son from the criminal world he inhabits shares The Immortal Man's central moral question: can a violent man protect his child from becoming what he is? Both films find genuine emotional power in the gangster-as-father archetype.
